newsitem.title: USA: Fed's changing of guard unlikely to affect policy.
newsitem.headline: Fed's changing of guard unlikely to affect policy.

text.p: The annual changing of the guard on a key Federal Reserve panel that sets interest rates could change the tenor of policy-makers' meetings next year but not necessarily the outcome, analysts said.
With economic growth moderate and inflation tame, the central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee is likely to continue to hold rates steady early next year.
The FOMC, which has not changed rates since January, meets for the last time this year on Tuesday.

Two tough-minded inflation fighters -- San Francisco Fed President Robert Parry and Richmond Fed chief Alfred Broaddus -- will become voting members of the FOMC in 1997 as part of the yearly rotation of positions on the 19-member panel.

Both men are outspoken Fed veterans who advocate making steady progress toward eliminating inflation -- in contrast to some of their colleagues who back an opportunistic approach that places a higher premium on short-term growth.
While there may be some lively discussions at the FOMC in 1997, most analysts are betting that the changes on the panel will not translate into a shift toward tighter monetary policy.

"I think the changing of guard on the FOMC is not going to make much of difference in policy, although we know it has certainly made a difference in the past," said former Fed Vice Chairman Preston Martin, now chairman of HomeVest Financial.
Both Parry and Broaddus have recently seemed less concerned about the inflation risks now facing the economy.
More importantly, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has seemed so too, and experts said that his views -- rather than those of other FOMC members -- ultimately carry the day.

The FOMC consists of Greenspan and six other Fed board governors in Washington, plus the presidents of the 12 regional Fed banks. Voting privileges for the bank presidents are rotated so that only five vote in any given year, although all of them take part in the discussions at every meeting.
In 1997, Parry, Broaddus, Michael Moskow of Chicago and Jack Guynn of Atlanta will vote. The head of the New York Fed, currently William McDonough, is a permanent voting member.

Experts expect Guynn to hold to a middle-of-the-road position while Moskow's likely stance is less certain. Martin, for one, believes that Moskow may be more inclined to raise rates, not because of a philosophical predilection, but because of a booming Midwest economy.
Gary Stern of Minneapolis, Cleveland's Jerry Jordan, Philadelphia's Edward Boehne and Robert McTeer of Dallas will lose their votes next year.
Stern voted against the Fed majority three times this year, arguing that higher rates were needed to cool off the economy and head off a rise in inflation.
So far, though, his fears have proved unfounded -- with underlying inflation moderating, rather than accelerating.
That has not been lost on either Parry or Broaddus. Parry told Reuters last month he had been pleasantly surprised by the inflation data, given the tightness in labour markets.
Broaddus also has appeared comfortable with recent events. In a speech Wednesday, he described the inflation numbers as encouraging and welcomed the recent moderation in growth.

"The fact that (the Fed bank presidents) are not clamouring for a tightening of monetary policy is understandable, given that we've had a distinct slowdown in growth," said former Fed Gov. Lyle Gramley, now with the Mortgage Bankers Association.

Roger Kubarych, general manager at Henry Kaufman and Co., said there seemed to be general agreement at the Fed on a "semi-permanent" strategy of avoiding changing rates until the data persuasively suggest a need to do so.

"I think there is a consensus not to move policy except as part of a series of moves. There is a feeling that if you are just at the borderline of a move, you're better off leaving things alone," he said. "For the time being, the Fed will be waiting regardless of who the individuals are on the FOMC."
